$$"] [17592186385927 :question/worked-solution "The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $8\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $20\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.1\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $10\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=20\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=20I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.1}=10q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=10\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=10\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
8\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)=20I+10q+10\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(8\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)) & =\frac{d}{dt}\left(20I+10q+10\,\frac{dI}{dt}\right) \\ -8\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & =20\,\frac{dI}{dt}+10\,\frac{dq}{dt}+10\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}+I=-\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${I}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{c}}{d{t}^{2}}+2\,\frac{d{I}_{c}}{dt}+{I}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-t}+Bt{e}^{-t},
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

- Next, we find a particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $t,$ i.e.,

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute this, as well as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d{I}_{p}}{dt} & =-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(t), \\ \frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{p}}{d{t}^{2}} & =-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t))+2(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)) \\ +(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t)) & =-\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ (2\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+(-2\alpha )\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & =-\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2\beta &=0\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)) \\ -2\alpha &=-\frac{4}{5}\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =\frac{2}{5}$ and $\beta =0.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)={I}_{c}(t)+{I}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-t}+Bt{e}^{-t}+\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-t}+Bt{e}^{-t}$ is the *transient current*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function ${I}_{p}(t)=\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)$ is the *steady-state current*. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
I(t)≈{I}_{p}(t)=\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state current, in amperes, is given by

$$
\sqrt{{\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)}^{2}+{0}^{2}}=\frac{2}{5}.
$$"] [17592186385934 :question/worked-solution "The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $13\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $4\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.25\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $1\,\text{H}.$

$$"] [17592186385954 :question/worked-solution "This Cauchy-Euler equation has non-polynomial forcing, but we are not given two fundamental solutions, so we cannot use variation of parameters.

$$"] [17592186385972 :question/worked-solution "First, we have

the equation of the tangent plane is

$$"] [17592186386480 :question/worked-solution "For a surface with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v),$ the fundamental vector product is defined as ${\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}.$

$$

Notice that the matrix ${P}^{2}$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. 
As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}-0.8 & 0.2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0.4 & -0.6 & 0.4 & 0 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & -0.4 & 0\end{array}\right] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=5{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=5{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=\frac{5}{2}{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}-4 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 & 0\end{array}\right] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 2 & -3 & 2 & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+4{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & -4 & 0\end{array}\right] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/ee/ee80e889e142c56b48a884a71dd714349ffbb95a6bdee3a3406679ed1edfaaa3.png)"] [17592186389126 :question/worked-solution "Notice that $x={y}^{3}+1\ge 0$ for all $y\in [0,1].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

where $f(y)={y}^{3}+1,$ and

$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′} & =\left\langle \frac{∂x}{∂y},\,\frac{∂y}{∂y}\,\frac{∂z}{∂y}\right\rangle =⟨{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,1,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =\left\langle \frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }\right\rangle =⟨-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}

and

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$"] [17592186391631 :question/worked-solution "First, we find ${\mathbf{g}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{g}}^{'}(t)‖:$

$$

It is known that

$$

where the functions $P$ and $Q$ are given by

$\,$ A suitable integrating factor is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The general solution is {{field-2}}, where $c$ is a constant."] [17592186391654 :question/worked-solution "For a differential equation of the form

$$

$$

we have that if

$$
\frac{1}{Q}\left(\frac{∂P}{∂y}-\frac{∂Q}{∂x}\right)=g(x)
$$

where $g(x)$ is independent of $y,$ then an integrating factor for the equation is

$$
I(x)=\operatorname{exp}⁡(\int g(x)\,\text{d}x)
$$

where $\operatorname{exp}⁡(x)$ denotes the exponential function ${e}^{x}.$

We are given that

$$
\frac{1}{Q}\left(\frac{∂P}{∂y}-\frac{∂Q}{∂x}\right)=\frac{1}{x}.
$$

Since $\frac{1}{x}$ is a function of $x$ only, we can conclude that the integrating factor for the equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int {x}^{-1}\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying our equation by the integrating factor, we arrive at the following exact differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x\left[(3x+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x+\left(xy+\frac{3}{x}\right)\,\text{d}y\right] & =0 \\ \underbrace{(3{x}^{2}+x{y}^{2})}_{\overset{~}{P}}\,\text{d}x+\underbrace{({x}^{2}y+3)}_{\overset{~}{Q}}\,\text{d}y & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

For this exact equation, we have

$$
\overset{~}{P}(x,y)=3{x}^{2}+x{y}^{2},\,\overset{~}{Q}(x,y)={x}^{2}y+3.
$$

To solve the equation, let's first integrate $\overset{~}{P}(x,y)$ with respect to $x.$
The result should include an arbitrary function of $y,$ which we'll call $F(y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(x,y) & =\int \overset{~}{P}(x,y)\,\text{d}x+F(y) \\  & =\int (3{x}^{2}+x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x+F(y) \\  & ={x}^{3}+\frac{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{2}+F(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, let's integrate $\overset{~}{Q}(x,y)$ with respect to $y.$
The result should include an arbitrary function of $x,$ which we'll call $G(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(x,y) & =\int \overset{~}{Q}(x,y)\,\text{d}y+G(x) \\  & =\int ({x}^{2}y+3)\,\text{d}y+G(x) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{2}+3y+G(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Comparing the two solutions, we must have

$$
F(y)=3y,\,G(x)={x}^{3}.

$$

$$"] [17592186392575 :question/worked-solution "To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to \infty .$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is ${x}^{3}.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by ${x}^{3},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{x+1}{1-{x}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{\left(\frac{x}{{x}^{3}}+\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\right)}{\left(\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}\right)} \\  & =\frac{\left(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\right)}{\left(\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}-1\right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}$ and $\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to \infty ,$ we have

$$

where $f$ and $g$ are differentiable functions of ${y}^{′}.$ 

In our case, we wish to transform the equation

$$
y=x\cdot \frac{1}{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

into a first-order linear equation for $x=x(t).$ We proceed in three steps:

**Step 1**: Substitute, and differentiate with respect to $x.$

We have the substitution

$$
t=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Substituting this into the equation gives

$$
y=x\cdot \frac{1}{t}+t.
$$

Differentiating both sides with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(x\cdot \frac{1}{t}+t\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the sum and product rules and using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(x\cdot \frac{1}{t}\right)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(t) \\ t & =\frac{1}{t}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)+x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{1}{t}\right)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(t) \\ t & =\frac{1}{t}-\frac{x}{{t}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}+\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Isolate the derivative and take its reciprocal.

We isolate $\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}t-\frac{1}{t} & =-\frac{x}{{t}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}+\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x} \\ \frac{{t}^{2}-1}{t} & =\left(\frac{{t}^{2}-x}{{t}^{2}}\right)\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x} \\ \frac{t({t}^{2}-1)}{{t}^{2}-x} & =\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}=\frac{t({t}^{2}-1)}{{t}^{2}-x}.
$$

Therefore, by taking the reciprocal of each side, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=\frac{{t}^{2}-x}{t({t}^{2}-1)}.
$$

**Step 3**: Express the derivative as a first-order linear equation.

Finally, we write this in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+P(t)x=Q(t)
$$

as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{{t}^{2}-x}{t({t}^{2}-1)} \\ t({t}^{2}-1)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & ={t}^{2}-x \\ t({t}^{2}-1)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x & ={t}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{x}{t({t}^{2}-1)} & =\frac{{t}^{2}}{t({t}^{2}-1)} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{x}{t({t}^{2}-1)} & =\frac{t}{{t}^{2}-1}\end{aligned}

$$"] [17592186367985 :question/problem "Calculate $\lim_{s\to 0}||f(s)||$, if $f(s)=⟨{e}^{s},\frac{{s}^{2}-2}{s+6},{4}^{s}⟩.$"] [17592186367985 :question/worked-solution "First, recall that:

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

- Statement “The point $(e,e)$ is a saddle point of $f$” is true. Indeed, since $H(e,e)<0,$ the point $(e,e)$ is a saddle point by the second partial derivative test.

 {{field-2}}"] [17592186370038 :question/worked-solution "Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${y}_{1}=0$ to ${y}_{2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{1}{1-{y}^{2}}\right))=\frac{2y}{1-{y}^{2}}\,⇒\,{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{2}=\frac{4{y}^{2}}{(1-{y}^{2})^{2}}.\end{aligned}

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1/\sqrt{2}}y\sqrt{1+\frac{4{y}^{2}}{(1-{y}^{2})^{2}}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1/\sqrt{2}}y\sqrt{\frac{(1+{y}^{2})^{2}}{(1-{y}^{2})^{2}}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1/\sqrt{2}}y\cdot \frac{1+{y}^{2}}{1-{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}

Finally, using the substitution 

$$

we get

$$

$$"] [17592186370846 :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is a continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.

For the surface $z=3$ for  $1\le x\le 2$ and $0\le y\le 1,$ the downward-pointing unit normal vector is

$$

Using the fact that $z=3$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨y,\,z,\,2x-y⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨y,\,3,\,2x-y⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-(2x-y).\end{aligned}

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}(-(2x-y))\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(2x-y))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2}(-(2x-y))\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}[({x}^{2}-xy){|}_{x=1}^{x=2}\,]\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}(3-y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{[3y-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186370866 :question/problem "Given that the polynomial $f(x)=2{x}^{3}+9{x}^{2}+7x-6$ has one of its roots in the interval $(0,\frac{3}{2}),$ find the sum of the distinct real roots of $f(x).$"] [17592186370866 :question/worked-solution "Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $-6$ and the leading coefficient is $2.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }-6}{\text{factor of }2}.
$$

Therefore, the possible rational roots are as follows:

$$
\pm \frac{1}{2},\,\pm \frac{3}{2},\,\pm 1,\,\pm 2,\,\pm 3,\,\pm 6
$$

Of these roots, the only roots in the interval $(0,\frac{3}{2}),$ are $\frac{1}{2}$ and $1.$

Now, let's use synthetic division to test whether $(x-\frac{1}{2})$ is a factor of $f(x).$ We get the following:

|  | $↓$ | $1$ | $5$ | $6$ |
|  | $2$ | $10$ | $12$ | $0$ |

Since the remainder is $0,$ we conclude that $(x-\frac{1}{2})$ is indeed a factor of $f(x).$ Moreover, we have

$$

Since the highest-degree factor is now a quadratic, we can continue factoring using the usual methods:

$$

Setting the factors equal to $0,$ we find the roots $x=\frac{1}{2},-2,-3.$ Summing these roots, we get

$$
\frac{1}{2}-2-3=-\frac{9}{2}.
$$"] [17592186370880 :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by

Hence, the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is

$$

Therefore, the radius of gyration about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}_{x} & =\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{M}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186370894 :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vectors of $U$ as ${\mathbf{u}}_{1},\hspace{0.167em}{\mathbf{u}}_{2}.$ To extend the given set to an orthogonal basis of ${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$, we need to find a third vector $\mathbf{x}=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}$ such that

$$

$$"] [17592186371021 :question/worked-solution "All of these vector-valued functions are defined at $t=0.$ 

A vector-valued function is differentiable at a point if and only if each of its components is differentiable at that point.

$$"] [17592186371180 :question/worked-solution "The variance of a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S$ is given by

$$
\text{Var}[X]={\sum }_{x\in S}(x-\text{E}[X])^{2}\cdot f(x).
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}y+2x=1\,⟹\,u=1,\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting $y-2x=v$ into the equation of the second line, we obtain

$$

$$

$$

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ is oriented upward, and

$$

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}19x-2{x}^{3}-2x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}-x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}18x-2{x}^{3}-2x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186372020 :question/worked-solution "Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the half-cone $z=-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ and the plane $z=-3.$ One such surface would be the plane $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=-3.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-3)=0 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-3)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨y,\hspace{0.222em}2yz,\hspace{0.222em}-{z}^{2}+1⟩{|}_{z=-3} \\  & =⟨\underbrace{y}_{P},\hspace{0.222em}\underbrace{-6y}_{Q},\hspace{0.222em}\underbrace{-8}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-y\cdot 0-(-6y)\cdot 0-8)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-8\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ with radius $3$ centered at the origin. Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta ,
$$

 

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}-8\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}-8\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-8{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \cdot {\int }_{0}^{3}r\,\text{d}r \\  & =-8[\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi }\cdot {[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{r=0}^{r=3} \\  & =-8(2\pi -0)\cdot (\frac{9}{2}-0) \\  & =-72\pi .\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186372027 :question/worked-solution "Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and the plane $z=2+2x-y.$ One such surface would be the plane $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=2+2x-y.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2+2x-y)=2 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2+2x-y)=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨-y,\hspace{0.222em}z,\hspace{0.222em}-2x⟩{|}_{z=2+2x-y} \\  & =⟨\underbrace{-y}_{P},\hspace{0.222em}\underbrace{2+2x-y}_{Q},\hspace{0.222em}\underbrace{-2x}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(-y)\cdot (2)-(2+2x-y)\cdot (-1)-2x)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2y+2+2x-y-2x)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2+y)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ with radius $1$ centered at the origin. Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta ,
$$

 

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2+y)\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}(2+r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}2r+{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[{r}^{2}+\frac{{r}^{3}}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(1+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={[\theta -\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186372125 :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux $$
\displaystyle {∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s
$$ along any closed curve $C\in D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}\in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

First, notice that

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(1-2x)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y)=-2+2=0,
$$

which shows that $F$ is a source-free vector field.

Since $F$ is source-free, we know the flux of $F$ is independent of the path. In particular, as we have that 

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where ${C}_{2}$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from $A$ to $B,$ and ${n}_{2}$ is the unit normal to ${C}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](images/21/212435c94989d0553db86b8d39edae3a7905d41ef668bb33fa0a62bed99d5462.png)

Notice that both ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $F$ across ${C}_{2},$ we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$

We have the parametrization

$$
r(t)=(-1)\,i+(2t-1)\,j,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =1-2x=1-2(-1)=3, \\ Q(x,y) & =2y=2(2t-1)=4t-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-1)=0, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-1)=2.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(3)\cdot (2)-(4t-2)\cdot (0)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6\,\text{d}t \\  & =6\cdot {[t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =6\cdot (1-0) \\  & =6\cdot 1 \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s=6.
$$"] [17592186372132 :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2}ky\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =k({\int }_{-1}^{1}\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{1}^{2}y\,\text{d}y) \\  & =k\cdot {[x]}_{-1}^{1}\cdot {[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =k(1-(-1))(2-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =3k.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\lambda (x,y)=ky=\frac{M}{3}y.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the line $x=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{l} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)[r(x,y)]^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{M}{3}y|x-1{|}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{M}{3}y(x-1)^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{M}{3}({\int }_{-1}^{1}(x-1)^{2}\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{1}^{2}y\,\text{d}y) \\  & =\frac{M}{3}\cdot {[\frac{1}{3}(x-1)^{3}]}_{-1}^{1}\cdot {[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{M}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{3}(0-(-8))\cdot [\frac{1}{2}(4-1)] \\  & =\frac{M}{3}\cdot \frac{8}{3}\cdot \frac{3}{2} \\  & =\frac{4M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186372251 :question/worked-solution "The moment of inertia of a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ about an axis of rotation $l$ is given by

$$
{I}_{l}={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)[r(x,y)]^{2}\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function of the lamina, and $r(x,y)$ is the distance from the line $l$ to the point $(x,y)$ on $D.$

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 1,\,\,1-{x}^{2}\le y\le 2-2{x}^{2}},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/02/026b560b2e81899cb767930a5c63173e4a3489c6bc10b7148007127e132406c9.png)

Also, the distance between a point and the line $x=-1$ is given by

$$
r(x,y)=|x+1|.
$$

Next, the mass density can be written as $\lambda (x,y)=k{x}^{2},$ where $k$ is a constant of proportionality. We can find the value of $k$ by integrating the mass density function over the plate.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{1-{x}^{2}}^{2-2{x}^{2}}k{x}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =k{\int }_{-1}^{1}{[{x}^{2}y]}_{1-{x}^{2}}^{2-2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =k{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{2}(2-2{x}^{2}-1+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =k{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{2}(1-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =k\cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{5}{x}^{5}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{4k}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\lambda (x,y)=k{x}^{2}=\frac{15}{4}M{x}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the line $x=-1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{l} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)[r(x,y)]^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{1-{x}^{2}}^{2-2{x}^{2}}\frac{15}{4}M{x}^{2}|x+1{|}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{1-{x}^{2}}^{2-2{x}^{2}}\frac{15}{4}M{x}^{2}(x+1)^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{15}{4}M{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{1-{x}^{2}}^{2-2{x}^{2}}({x}^{4}+2{x}^{3}+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{15}{4}M{\int }_{-1}^{1}({x}^{4}+2{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}){\int }_{1-{x}^{2}}^{2-2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{15}{4}M{\int }_{-1}^{1}({x}^{4}+2{x}^{3}+{x}^{2})[y]_{1-{x}^{2}}^{2-2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{15}{4}M{\int }_{-1}^{1}({x}^{4}+2{x}^{3}+{x}^{2})(1-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{15}{4}M{\int }_{-1}^{1}(-{x}^{6}-2{x}^{5}+2{x}^{3}+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{15}{4}M{[-\frac{1}{7}{x}^{7}-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{6}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{4}+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{15}{4}M(-\frac{2}{7}+0+0+\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =\frac{15}{4}M\cdot \frac{8}{21} \\  & =\frac{10M}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186372272 :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina of mass $M$ and a line ${l}_{M}$ perpendicular to the lamina passing through its center of mass, the parallel axis theorem states that the moment of inertia of the lamina about a line $l$ parallel to ${l}_{M}$ is given by

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=4\cdot 6=24\,{\text{m}}^{2}.$
Since the plate has a uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$

and its center of mass is its centroid:

Since the center of mass is at the origin, the moment of inertia about the perpendicular line through the center of mass is

$$"] [17592186372286 :question/problem "A rectangular plate occupies the region

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=13\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=13I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.2}=5q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=6\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=6\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
10=13I+5q+6\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(10) & =\frac{d}{dt}(13I+5q+6\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ 0 & =13\,\frac{dI}{dt}+5\,\frac{dq}{dt}+6\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+\frac{13}{6}\cdot \frac{dI}{dt}+\frac{5}{6}I=0.
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must take a linear combination of two linearly independent solutions.

Assuming the solutions take the form $I={e}^{\lambda t},$ we obtain two solutions, namely, $I={e}^{-5t/3}$ and $I={e}^{-t/2}.$
So, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)=A{e}^{-5t/3}+B{e}^{-t/2}.
$$

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of $\frac{2}{5}\,\text{C}$ on the capacitor and an initial current of $\frac{3}{2}\,\text{A}.$
Now, solving the Kirchhoff's law equation for $\frac{dI}{dt},$ we have

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}=\frac{5}{3}-\frac{13}{6}I-\frac{5}{6}q.
$$

So, we can apply the initial conditions $I(0)=\frac{3}{2}$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(0) & =\frac{5}{3}-\frac{13}{6}I(0)-\frac{5}{6}q(0) \\  & =\frac{5}{3}-\frac{13}{6}\cdot \frac{3}{2}-\frac{5}{6}\cdot \frac{2}{5} \\  & =-\frac{23}{12},\end{aligned}
$$

and solve for $A$ and $B.$

- Substituting $I(0)=\frac{3}{2}$ into our general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2} & =A{e}^{-5(0)/3}+B{e}^{-0/2} \\ \frac{3}{2} & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $I,$ we get

$$
{I}^{′}=-\frac{5}{3}A{e}^{-5t/3}-\frac{1}{2}B{e}^{-t/2}
$$

Substituting in ${I}^{′}(0)=-\frac{23}{12}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{23}{12} & =-\frac{5}{3}A{e}^{-5(0)/3}-\frac{1}{2}B{e}^{-0/2} \\ -\frac{23}{12} & =-\frac{5}{3}A-\frac{1}{2}B.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the two equations in $A$ and $B$ together gives the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2} &=A+B \\ -\frac{23}{12} &=-\frac{5}{3}A-\frac{1}{2}B\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $A=1$ and $B=\frac{1}{2}.$ Therefore, the equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit is

$$
I(t)={e}^{-5t/3}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-t/2}.
$$

Finally, the current in the circuit after $0.3$ seconds, in amperes, is

$$
I(0.3)={e}^{-5(0.3)/3}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-(0.3)/2}≈1.037,
$$

$$

Let's define a transformation $\mathbf{T}$ as follows: 

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=x-y,\,v=y+1

gives us the *inverse* function ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{\mathbf{T}}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-y)^{2}+y=2\,⟹\,(y+1)=3-(x-y)^{2}\,⟹\,v=3-{u}^{2},\end{aligned}

while substituting $y=v-1$ into the equation of the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y=0\,⟹\,v=1.\end{aligned}

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}v &=3-{u}^{2} \\ v &=1\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}u &=\pm \sqrt{2} \\ v &=1.\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}

So, the intersection points are $(\pm \sqrt{2},1).$

$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}$ is

Therefore, we conclude that $y(2)≈\frac{19}{12}.$"] [17592186374780 :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the mass of fertilizer in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes. This is equal to the rate at which fertilizer enters the tank minus the rate at which fertilizer leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{g}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which fertilizer enters the tank.

First, note that a water solution containing $25\,\text{g/L}$ of fertilizer enters the tank at a rate of $6\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *fertilizer* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(25\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{L}})\cdot (6\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(25\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (6\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =150\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which fertilizer exits the tank.

Now, to find the rate at which fertilizer leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of water in the tank at time $t.$

- The tank initially contains $800\,\text{L}$ of water.

- A solution enters the tank at a rate of $6\,\text{L/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $6t\,\text{L}$ have entered the tank.

- The completely mixed water solution leaves the tank at a rate of $10\,\text{L/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $10t\,\text{L}$ have left the tank.

As a result, the volume of water in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
800+6t-10t=800-4t\,\text{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the amount of fertilizer in the tank, the *concentration* of the water solution at time $t$ is 

$$
\frac{Q}{800-4t}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{L}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed water leaves at a rate of $10\,\text{L/min},$ *fertilizer* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(10\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{800-4t}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(10\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{800-4t}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{10Q}{800-4t}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

Finally, the rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =150-\frac{10Q}{800-4t}\end{aligned}
$$

which finally gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{10}{800-4t}Q=150.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186374787 :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative

\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{3}{80+t} \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\int \left(-\frac{3}{80+t}\right)\,dt \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \,dQ & =-3\int \frac{1}{80+t}\,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-3\operatorname{ln}⁡|80+t|+C \\ |Q| & ={e}^{-3\operatorname{ln}⁡|80+t|+C} \\ Q(t) & =\frac{A}{(80+t)^{3}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $A=\pm {e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the basin initially contains $12\,\text{lb}$ of contaminants. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=12,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =12 \\ \frac{A}{(80+0)^{3}} & =12 \\ A & =12\cdot {80}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
Q(t)=12{\left(\frac{80}{80+t}\right)}^{3}
$$

Finally, the amount of contaminants in the basin $10$ minutes after the clean water is first pumped in is

$$
Q(12)=12{\left(\frac{80}{90}\right)}^{3}≈8.43\,\text{lb},
$$

rounded to two decimal places."] [17592186374847 :question/worked-solution "Let $Q$ be the amount of salt in the tank at time $t.$ Then, the derivative 

$$

$$

$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which salt enters the tank.

First, note that fresh water (i.e., a brine solution containing $0\,\text{lb/gal}$ of salt) enters the tank at a rate of $3\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *salt* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (3\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (3\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which salt exits the tank.

To find the rate at which salt leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of brine in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $150\,\text{gal}$ of brine; fresh water enters at $3\,\text{gal/min},$ and mixed brine leaves at $2\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of brine in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=150+3t-2t=(150+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the tank, the concentration of the brine at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{150+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed brine leaves at a rate of $2\,\text{gal/min},$ *salt* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(2\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{150+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(2\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{150+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{2Q}{150+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0-\frac{2Q}{150+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}=-\frac{2}{150+t}\,Q.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{2}{150+t} \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\int \left(-\frac{2}{150+t}\right)\,dt \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \,dQ & =-2\int \frac{1}{150+t}\,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-2(\operatorname{ln}⁡|150+t|)+C \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(150+t)^{-2}|+C \\ |Q| & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|(150+t)^{-2}|+C} \\ Q(t) & =\frac{A}{(150+t)^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $A=\pm {e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the tank initially contains $32\,\text{lb}$ of salt. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=32,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =32 \\ \frac{A}{(150+0)^{2}} & =32 \\ A & =32(150)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =\frac{32(150)^{2}}{(150+t)^{2}} \\  & =32{\left(\frac{150}{150+t}\right)}^{2}\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(90) & =32{\left(\frac{150}{150+90}\right)}^{2} \\  & =32{\left(\frac{150}{240}\right)}^{2} \\  & =32{\left(\frac{5}{8}\right)}^{2} \\  & =12.5\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186374854 :question/worked-solution "Let $Q$ be the amount of reactant in the reactor at time $t.$ Then, the derivative

rounded to two decimal places."] [17592186374993 :question/worked-solution "The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

First, recall that, by definition

$$
\operatorname{sinh}⁡(5t)=\frac{{e}^{5t}-{e}^{-5t}}{2}.
$$

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(5t)} & =L{\frac{{e}^{5t}-{e}^{-5t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{5t}}{2}-\frac{{e}^{-5t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{5t}}{2}}-L{\frac{{e}^{-5t}}{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{5t}}-\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-5t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall that 

$$
L{{e}^{kt}}=\frac{1}{s-k},\,s>k.
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{5t}} & =\frac{1}{s-5},\,s>5 \\ L{{e}^{-5t}} & =\frac{1}{s+5},\,s>-5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{sinh}⁡(5t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(5t)} & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{5t}}-\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-5t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s-5}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s+5} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{s-5}-\frac{1}{s+5}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{(s+5)-(s-5)}{(s-5)(s+5)}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{10}{{s}^{2}-25}\right) \\  & =\frac{5}{{s}^{2}-25}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $L{{e}^{5t}}$ is defined for $s\in (5,\infty )$ and $L{{e}^{-5t}}$ is defined for $s\in (-5,\infty ),$ we have that $L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(5t)}$ is defined for

$$
(5,\infty )\cap (-5,\infty )=(5,\infty ),
$$

that is, $s>5.$"] [17592186375028 :question/worked-solution "We define the following variables:

- let $L,$ $W,$ and $H$ be the length, width, and height of the bread loaf, respectively, and

- let $V$ be the volume of the bread loaf.

We are given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L=100\text{ mm},\, & W=60\text{ mm}, \\ H=30\text{ mm},\, & \frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}t}=-2\text{ mm/s}, \\ \frac{\text{d}H}{\text{d}t}=1\text{ mm/s}\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.$

The relation between the three time-dependent variables, $V,$ $H$ and $L,$ is given by the formula for the volume of bread loaf:

$$
V=LWH
$$

We differentiate both sides of $V=LWH$ with respect to $t,$ treating $W$ as a constant, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}V & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(LWH) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =W\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(LH) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =W[L\left(\frac{\text{d}H}{\text{d}t}\right)+H\left(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}t}\right)] \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =W\cdot L\left(\frac{\text{d}H}{\text{d}t}\right)+W\cdot H\left(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}t}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can plug in the known values and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =(60)(100)(1)+(60)(30)(-2) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =6000-3600 \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =2400.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of bread loaf is increasing at a rate of $2400\,{\text{mm}}^{3}\text{/s}.$"] [17592186375031 :question/worked-solution "Suppose that $f(x)$ is a $2L$-periodic piecewise smooth function with the corresponding Fourier series

$$
S(x)=\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x).
$$

Then, the series converges for all $x\in R.$

- If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x,$ then the series converges to the value of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=f(x)
$$

- If $f(x)$ has a jump discontinuity at $x,$ then the series converges to the midpoint between the values of left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=\frac{{f}^{-}(x)+{f}^{+}(x)}{2}
$$

where ${f}^{-}(x)$ and ${f}^{+}(x)$ are the left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point, respectively.

First, note that a solution containing $0.5\,\text{lb/gal}$ of inhibitor enters the reservoir at a rate of $21\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *inhibitor* enters the reservoir is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.5\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (21\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.5\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (21\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =10.5\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which inhibitor exits the reservoir.

To find the rate at which inhibitor leaves the reservoir, we must first determine the volume of solution in the reservoir at time $t.$

The reservoir initially contains $70\,\text{gal}$ of solution; solution enters at $21\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $14\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the reservoir after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=70+21t-14t=7(10+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the reservoir is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of inhibitor in the reservoir, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{7(10+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $14\,\text{gal/min},$ *inhibitor* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(14\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{7(10+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(14\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{7(10+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{14Q}{7(10+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{10+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =10.5-\frac{2Q}{10+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{10+t}\,Q=10.5.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(10+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|10+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(10+t)^{2}} \\  & =(10+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(10+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(10+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{10+t}\,Q) & =(10+t)^{2}\cdot 10.5 \\ (10+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(10+t)Q & =10.5(10+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(10+t)^{2}) & =10.5(10+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(10+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 10.5(10+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(10+t)^{2} & =10.5\cdot \frac{1}{3}(10+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =3.5(10+t)+\frac{C}{(10+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the reservoir initially contains $20\,\text{lb}$ of inhibitor. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=20,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =20 \\ 3.5(10+0)+\frac{C}{(10+0)^{2}} & =20 \\ 35+\frac{C}{(10)^{2}} & =20 \\ \frac{C}{{10}^{2}} & =-15 \\ C & =-15(10)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =3.5(10+t)-\frac{15(10)^{2}}{(10+t)^{2}} \\  & =3.5(10+t)-15{\left(\frac{10}{10+t}\right)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the reservoir begins to overflow. The reservoir has a capacity of $210\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=210$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =210 \\ 70+21{t}_{o}-14{t}_{o} & =210 \\ 70+7{t}_{o} & =210 \\ 7{t}_{o} & =140 \\ {t}_{o} & =20\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of inhibitor in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(20) & =3.5(10+20)-15{\left(\frac{10}{10+20}\right)}^{2} \\  & =105-15{\left(\frac{10}{30}\right)}^{2} \\  & ≈103.3\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186377205 :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of flavoring in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which flavoring enters the tank minus the rate at which flavoring leaves the tank.

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{25+t}\,Q=6.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(25+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|25+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(25+t)^{2}} \\  & =(25+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(25+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(25+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{25+t}\,Q) & =(25+t)^{2}\cdot 6 \\ (25+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(25+t)Q & =6(25+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(25+t)^{2}) & =6(25+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(25+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 6(25+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(25+t)^{2} & =6\cdot \frac{1}{3}(25+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =2(25+t)+\frac{C}{(25+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the tank initially contains $25\,\text{lb}$ of flavoring. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=25,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =25 \\ 2(25+0)+\frac{C}{(25+0)^{2}} & =25 \\ 50+\frac{C}{(25)^{2}} & =25 \\ \frac{C}{{25}^{2}} & =-25 \\ C & =-25(25)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =2(25+t)-\frac{25(25)^{2}}{(25+t)^{2}} \\  & =2(25+t)-25{\left(\frac{25}{25+t}\right)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $150\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=150$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =150 \\ 75+9{t}_{o}-6{t}_{o} & =150 \\ 75+3{t}_{o} & =150 \\ 3{t}_{o} & =75 \\ {t}_{o} & =25\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of flavoring in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(25) & =2(25+25)-25{\left(\frac{25}{25+25}\right)}^{2} \\  & =100-25{\left(\frac{25}{50}\right)}^{2} \\  & ≈93.8\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186377212 :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of disinfectant in the reservoir at time $t,$ the derivative

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =12-\frac{2Q}{10+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{10+t}\,Q=12.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(10+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|10+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(10+t)^{2}} \\  & =(10+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(10+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(10+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{10+t}\,Q) & =(10+t)^{2}\cdot 12 \\ (10+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(10+t)Q & =12(10+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(10+t)^{2}) & =12(10+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(10+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 12(10+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(10+t)^{2} & =12\cdot \frac{1}{3}(10+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =4(10+t)+\frac{C}{(10+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}

We're told that the reservoir initially contains $10\,\text{lb}$ of disinfectant. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=10,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =10 \\ 4(10+0)+\frac{C}{(10+0)^{2}} & =10 \\ 40+\frac{C}{(10)^{2}} & =10 \\ \frac{C}{{10}^{2}} & =-30 \\ C & =-30(10)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =4(10+t)-\frac{30(10)^{2}}{(10+t)^{2}} \\  & =4(10+t)-30{\left(\frac{10}{10+t}\right)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the reservoir begins to overflow. The reservoir has a capacity of $200\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=200$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =200 \\ 50+15{t}_{o}-10{t}_{o} & =200 \\ 50+5{t}_{o} & =200 \\ 5{t}_{o} & =150 \\ {t}_{o} & =30\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of disinfectant in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(30) & =4(10+30)-30{\left(\frac{10}{10+30}\right)}^{2} \\  & =160-30{\left(\frac{10}{40}\right)}^{2} \\  & ≈158.1\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186377228 :question/worked-solution "First, notice that the unit tangent and the principal normal at the point where $t=1$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}T(1) & =\frac{1}{1+1}(i+1\,j+\sqrt{2}k)=\frac{1}{2}(i+j+\sqrt{2}k) \\ N(1) & =\frac{1}{1+1}(-\sqrt{2}\,i+\sqrt{2}\,j+(1-1)k)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(-i+j).\end{aligned}
$$

Also, the position vector of the point  where $t=1$ is

$$
p=r(1)=6\,i+2\,j+3\sqrt{2}\,k.
$$

Now, we need to find a vector that's perpendicular to the osculating plane. To do that, we use the cross product of the unit tangent $T(1)$ and the principal normal $N(1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =T(1)\times N(1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(i+j+\sqrt{2}k)k\times (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(-i+j)) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & \sqrt{2} \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\left[\text{ }\begin{vmatrix}1 & \sqrt{2} \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix}\,i-\begin{vmatrix}1 & \sqrt{2} \\ -1 & 0\end{vmatrix}\,j+\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{vmatrix}\,k\text{ }\right] \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}⟨-\sqrt{2},-\sqrt{2},2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{2}⟨-1,-1,\sqrt{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the shortest distance between our plane and the origin is given by

$$
d=\frac{|(p-0)\cdot n|}{‖n‖}=\frac{|p\cdot n|}{‖n‖}=|p\cdot n|,
$$

since $‖n‖=1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|p\cdot n| \\  & =|⟨6,2,3\sqrt{2}⟩\cdot \frac{1}{2}⟨-1,-1,\sqrt{2}⟩| \\  & =\frac{1}{2}|-6-2+6| \\  & =1.\end{aligned}

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively."] [17592186377235 :question/worked-solution "First, notice that the unit tangent and the principal normal at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ are

Now, we need to find a vector that's perpendicular to the osculating plane. To do that, we use the cross product of the unit tangent $T\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)$ and the principal normal $N\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right):$

$$
\begin{aligned}T\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)\times N\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & =⟨-1,0,0⟩\times (-\frac{1}{5}⟨0,3,4⟩) \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\left[\text{ }\begin{vmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 3 & 4\end{vmatrix}\,i-\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{vmatrix}\,j+\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{vmatrix}\,k\text{ }\right] \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}⟨0,4,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since we are interested only in the direction of the above vector, let's write our perpendicular vector $n$ as 

$$
n=(-5)\cdot (T\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)\times N\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right))=⟨0,4,-3⟩.
$$

Finally, let $⟨x,y,z⟩$ denote the position vector of a point on the osculating plane. Since the plane is perpendicular to $n$ and passes through the tip of the position vector $p$, its Cartesian equation can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}(⟨x,y,z⟩-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n-p\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨0,4,-3⟩ & =⟨0,3,4⟩\cdot ⟨0,4,-3⟩ \\ 0\cdot x+4\cdot y+(-3)\cdot z & =0 \\ 4y-3z & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186377242 :question/worked-solution "Let $Q$ be the amount of supplement in the tank at time $t,$ in minutes. Then, the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t.$ This is equal to the rate at which supplements enter the tank minus the rate at which supplements leave the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which supplements enter the tank.

Note that a feed solution containing $0.03\,\text{kg/L}$ of the supplement enters the tank at a rate of $12\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *supplement* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.03\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (12\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.03\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (12\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0.36\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which supplements exit the tank.

Next, note that the rate of flow in equals the rate of flow out, so the volume in the tank remains $720\,\text{L}.$ Then, since $Q$ is the amount of supplement in the tank, the *concentration* of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{720}\,\text{kg/L}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of $12\,\text{L/min},$ *supplement* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(12\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{720}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(12\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{720}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{12Q}{720}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{Q}{60}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0.36-\frac{Q}{60}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{1}{60}Q=0.36.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${Q}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{Q}_{c}}{dt}+\frac{1}{60}{Q}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{Q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-t/60},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $0.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $0,$ i.e.,

$$
{Q}_{p}(t)=\alpha .
$$

To find the value of $\alpha ,$ we substitute ${Q}_{p}=\alpha $ and $\frac{d{Q}_{p}}{dt}=(\alpha )^{′}=0$ into the inhomogeneous equation:

$$
0+\frac{1}{60}\alpha =0.36\,⟹\,\alpha =21.6.
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is ${Q}_{p}(t)=21.6.$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
Q(t)={Q}_{c}(t)+{Q}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-t/60}+21.6.
$$

We're told that the tank initially contains $3\,\text{kg}$ of dissolved supplement. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=3,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =3 \\ A{e}^{-0/60}+21.6 & =3 \\ A & =-18.6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
Q(t)=21.6-18.6{e}^{-t/60}
$$

Finally,  the amount of supplement in the tank $5$ minutes after pumping begins is

$$

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t.$ This is equal to the rate at which preservative enters the tank minus the rate at which preservative leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which preservative enters the tank.

Note that a feed solution containing $0.05\,\text{kg/L}$ of the preservative enters the tank at a rate of $18\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *preservative* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.05\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (18\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.05\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (18\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0.9\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which preservative exits the tank.

To find the rate at which preservative leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of liquid in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $420\,\text{L}$ of liquid; a solution enters at $18\,\text{L/min}$ and leaves at $12\,\text{L/min}.$
As a result, the volume of liquid in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
420+18t-12t=(420+6t)\,\text{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the amount of preservative in the tank, the *concentration* of the mixed solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{420+6t}\,\text{kg/L}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of $12\,\text{L/min},$ *preservative* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(12\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{420+6t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(12\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{420+6t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{12Q}{420+6t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{70+t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0.9-\frac{2Q}{70+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{70+t}Q=0.9.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(70+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|70+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(70+t)^{2}} \\  & =(70+t)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(70+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(70+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{70+t}Q) & =(70+t)^{2}\cdot 0.9 \\ (70+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(70+t)Q & =0.9(70+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(70+t)^{2}) & =0.9(70+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(70+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 0.9(70+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(70+t)^{2} & =0.9\cdot \frac{1}{3}(70+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =0.3(70+t)+\frac{C}{(70+t)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the tank initially contains $10\,\text{kg}$ of preservative. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=10,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =10 \\ 0.3(70+0)+\frac{C}{(70+0)^{2}} & =10 \\ 21+\frac{C}{{70}^{2}} & =10 \\ \frac{C}{{70}^{2}} & =-11 \\ C & =-11(70)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =0.3(70+t)-\frac{11(70)^{2}}{(70+t)^{2}} \\  & =0.3(70+t)-11{\left(\frac{70}{70+t}\right)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,  the amount of preservative in the tank $15$ minutes after pumping begins is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(15) & =0.3(70+15)-11{\left(\frac{70}{70+15}\right)}^{2} \\  & =25.5-11{\left(\frac{70}{85}\right)}^{2} \\  & ≈18.04\,\text{kg},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places."] [17592186377256 :question/worked-solution "Let $Q$ be the amount of additive in the tank at time $t,$ in minutes. Then, the derivative

where $\lambda $ and ${a}_{n}$ for $n=0,1,2,…$ are constants.

Substituting this solution and its derivatives into the ODE, collecting like terms, and setting coefficients equal to zero, we obtain:

- the indicial equation from the coefficients of the $n=0$ term for arbitrary ${a}_{0},$ and

- a recurrence formula from the coefficients of the $n\ge 1$ terms.

$$
\begin{aligned}4x{y}^{″} & =4({\lambda }^{2}-\lambda ){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda -1}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }4((\lambda +n)^{2}-(\lambda +n)){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n-1}, \\ {y}^{′} & =\lambda {a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda -1}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(\lambda +n){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n-1} \\ 5y & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }5{a}_{n-1}{x}^{\lambda +n-1}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}4({\lambda }^{2}-\lambda ){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda -1}+\lambda {a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda -1} &= (4{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +\lambda ){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda -1} \\ &= (4{\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda ){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda -1}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$"] [17592186377391 :question/worked-solution "If $x=0$ is a regular singular point of a second-order homogeneous linear differential equation, then the method of Frobenius states that there is at least one solution of the form
