\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ {x}^{2} & xz & {z}^{2}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =[\frac{∂}{∂y}({z}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂z}(xz)]\mathbf{i}-[\frac{∂}{∂x}({z}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2})]\mathbf{j}+[\frac{∂}{∂x}(xz)-\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2})]\mathbf{k} \\  & =(0-x)\mathbf{i}-(0-0)\mathbf{j}+(z-0)\mathbf{k} \\  & =-x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+z\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}$ at the point $(-2,-3,1),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F})(-2,-3,1) & =-(-2)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186383272 :question/worked-solution "If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+R\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$ is a vector field on ${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $\mathbf{F}$ all exist, then the curl of $\mathbf{F}$ is the vector field given by

$$
\operatorname{curl} \hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}=\mathrm{∇}\times \mathbf{F}=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ P & Q & R\end{vmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ 2xy+2z & {y}^{2}+1 & x+y\end{vmatrix} \\  & =[\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y)-\frac{∂}{∂z}({y}^{2}+1)]\mathbf{i}-[\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+y)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(2xy+2z)]\mathbf{j}+[\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+1)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy+2z)]\mathbf{k} \\  & =(1-0)\mathbf{i}-(1-2)\mathbf{j}+(0-2x)\mathbf{k} \\  & =\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}-2x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}$ at the point $(-3,0,-1),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F})(-3,0,-1) & =\mathbf{i}+\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}-2(-3)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+6\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186383314 :question/problem "The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Given that the point $P(\frac{\pi }{2},1,0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}y)$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$"] [17592186383314 :question/worked-solution "The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(\frac{\pi }{2},1).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(\frac{\pi }{2},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(\frac{\pi }{2},1) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 1)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 1) \\  & =2\cdot 1-0 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(\frac{\pi }{2},1) & ={f}_{y}(\frac{\pi }{2},1)(y-1) \\ z-0 & =2(y-1) \\ z & =2y-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\frac{\pi }{2},1,0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=\frac{\pi }{2} \\ z &=2y-2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ a normal vector to the plane is ${\mathbf{n}}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=2y-2$ (or $2y-z-2=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${\mathbf{n}}_{2}=⟨0,2,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,2,-1⟩ \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =j+2\,k \\  & =⟨0,1,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $⟨0,1,2⟩.$"] [17592186383515 :question/worked-solution "Given a transformation 

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T},$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)$ and $y(u,v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v).$ 

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v) & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v) & -\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v)\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v))\cdot (-\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v))-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v))\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\pi /4 \\ \pi /4\end{bmatrix},$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is 

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{4})}=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=2.
$$"] [17592186384051 :question/worked-solution "We need to express the summation $S(k+1)$ in terms of $S(k).$

Let ${a}_{i}$ for $i\ge 0$ be a sequence, and let $S(k)$ denote the sum of the first $k+1$ terms.

$$
S(k)={\sum }_{i=0}^{k}{a}_{i}
$$

We can always express $S(k+1)$ in terms of $S(k)$ by writing the last term on its own, as follows: 

$$
{\sum }_{i=0}^{k+1}{a}_{i}=({\sum }_{i=0}^{k}{a}_{i})+{a}_{k+1}.
$$

In our case, we have ${a}_{i}=\frac{1}{{3}^{i}}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{k+1}=\frac{1}{{3}^{k+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
{\sum }_{i=0}^{k+1}\frac{1}{{3}^{i}}=({\sum }_{i=0}^{k}\frac{1}{{3}^{i}})+\left(\frac{1}{{3}^{k+1}}\right),
$$

which we can write as 

$$
S(k+1)=S(k)+\frac{1}{{3}^{k+1}}.
$$"] [17592186384656 :question/worked-solution "Let $u={\log }_{5}⁡({x}^{3}).$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\,⟹\,\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}{3}\text{d}u=\frac{\text{d}x}{x}.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\log }_{5}⁡({x}^{3})}{2x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int {\log }_{5}⁡({x}^{3})\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{x} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int u\cdot (\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}{3}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}{6}\int u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}{6}\cdot \frac{{u}^{2}}{2}+C \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡5{\log }_{5}^{2}⁡({x}^{3})}{12}+C.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186385155 :question/worked-solution "Notice that we can rewrite the series as follows:

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{4}\frac{12}{{8}^{n}}={\sum }_{n=1}^{4}12\cdot {\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)}^{n}
$$

Since the above series is in the form $$
\displaystyle {\sum }_{n=1}^{N}a{r}^{n},
$$ it is a geometric series. 

To determine the sum, we use the formula for the sum ${S}_{N}$ of a geometric series.

$$
{S}_{N}={a}_{1}\frac{(1-{r}^{N})}{1-r}
$$

In this case, $r=\frac{1}{8}$ and $N=4.$ We need to figure out ${a}_{1}.$

The formula for the $n$th term of the series is

$$
{a}_{n}=12\cdot {\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)}^{n},
$$

and therefore the first term of the series is

$$
{a}_{1}=12\cdot {\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)}^{1}=\frac{3}{2}.
$$

If we substitute ${a}_{1}=\frac{3}{2},r=\frac{1}{8}$ and $N=4$ into the formula for ${S}_{N}$, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{5}12\cdot {\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)}^{n} & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{[1-{\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)}^{4}]}{(1-\frac{1}{8})} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{(1-\frac{1}{4096})}{\frac{7}{8}} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{8}{7}\cdot \frac{4095}{4096} \\  & =\frac{1755}{1024}\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186385161 :question/worked-solution "Since the given series is in the form $$
\displaystyle {\sum }_{n=1}^{N}a{r}^{n},
$$ it is a geometric series. 

To determine the sum, we use the formula for the sum ${S}_{N}$ of a geometric series.

$$
{S}_{N}={a}_{1}\frac{(1-{r}^{N})}{1-r}
$$

In this case, $r=\frac{1}{4}$ and $N=4.$ We need to figure out the value of ${a}_{1}.$

The formula for the $n$th term of the series is

$$
{a}_{n}=10{\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)}^{n},
$$

and therefore, we can calculate the first term ${a}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & =10{\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)}^{1} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

If we substitute ${a}_{1}=\frac{5}{2},r=\frac{1}{4}$ and $N=4$ into the formula for ${S}_{N}$, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{4}10{\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)}^{n} & =\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{(1-{\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)}^{4})}{(1-\frac{1}{4})} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{(1-\frac{1}{256})}{\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{\left(\frac{255}{256}\right)}{\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)} \\  & =\frac{425}{128}\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186385208 :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of dye in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which dye enters the tank minus the rate at which dye leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which dye enters the tank.

First, note that a solution containing $0.6\,\text{lb/gal}$ of dye enters the tank at a rate of $15\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *dye* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.6\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (15\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.6\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (15\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =9\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which dye exits the tank.

To find the rate at which dye leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of liquid in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $100\,\text{gal}$ of liquid; solution enters at $15\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $10\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of liquid in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=100+15t-10t=5(20+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of dye in the tank, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{5(20+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $10\,\text{gal/min},$ *dye* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(10\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{5(20+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(10\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{5(20+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{10Q}{5(20+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{20+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =9-\frac{2Q}{20+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{20+t}\,Q=9.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(20+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|20+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(20+t)^{2}} \\  & =(20+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(20+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(20+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{20+t}\,Q) & =(20+t)^{2}\cdot 9 \\ (20+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(20+t)Q & =9(20+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(20+t)^{2}) & =9(20+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(20+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 9(20+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(20+t)^{2} & =9\cdot \frac{1}{3}(20+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =3(20+t)+\frac{C}{(20+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the tank initially contains $20\,\text{lb}$ of dye. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=20,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =20 \\ 3(20+0)+\frac{C}{(20+0)^{2}} & =20 \\ 60+\frac{C}{(20)^{2}} & =20 \\ \frac{C}{(20)^{2}} & =-40 \\ C & =-40(20)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =3(20+t)-\frac{40(20)^{2}}{(20+t)^{2}} \\  & =3(20+t)-40{\left(\frac{20}{20+t}\right)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $180\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=180$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =180 \\ 100+15{t}_{o}-10{t}_{o} & =180 \\ 100+5{t}_{o} & =180 \\ 5{t}_{o} & =80 \\ {t}_{o} & =16\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of dye in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(16) & =3(20+16)-40{\left(\frac{20}{20+16}\right)}^{2} \\  & =108-40{\left(\frac{20}{36}\right)}^{2} \\  & ≈95.7\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186385215 :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the reservoir at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which salt enters the reservoir minus the rate at which salt leaves the reservoir.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which salt enters the reservoir.

First, note that a solution containing $1.0\,\text{lb/gal}$ of salt enters the reservoir at a rate of $6\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *salt* enters the reservoir is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(1.0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (6\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(1.0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (6\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =6\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which salt exits the reservoir.

To find the rate at which salt leaves the reservoir, we must first determine the volume of solution in the reservoir at time $t.$

The reservoir initially contains $100\,\text{gal}$ of solution; solution enters at $6\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $4\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the reservoir after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=100+6t-4t=2(50+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the reservoir is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the reservoir, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{2(50+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $4\,\text{gal/min},$ *salt* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(4\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{2(50+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(4\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{2(50+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{4Q}{2(50+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{50+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =6-\frac{2Q}{50+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{50+t}\,Q=6.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(50+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|50+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(50+t)^{2}} \\  & =(50+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(50+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(50+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{50+t}\,Q) & =(50+t)^{2}\cdot 6 \\ (50+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(50+t)Q & =6(50+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(50+t)^{2}) & =6(50+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(50+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 6(50+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(50+t)^{2} & =6\cdot \frac{1}{3}(50+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =2(50+t)+\frac{C}{(50+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the reservoir initially contains $25\,\text{lb}$ of salt. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=25,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =25 \\ 2(50+0)+\frac{C}{(50+0)^{2}} & =25 \\ 100+\frac{C}{(50)^{2}} & =25 \\ \frac{C}{(50)^{2}} & =-75 \\ C & =-75(50)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =2(50+t)-\frac{75(50)^{2}}{(50+t)^{2}} \\  & =2(50+t)-75{\left(\frac{50}{50+t}\right)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the reservoir begins to overflow. The reservoir has a capacity of $160\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=160$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =160 \\ 100+6{t}_{o}-4{t}_{o} & =160 \\ 100+2{t}_{o} & =160 \\ 2{t}_{o} & =60 \\ {t}_{o} & =30\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of salt in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(30) & =2(50+30)-75{\left(\frac{50}{50+30}\right)}^{2} \\  & =160-75{\left(\frac{50}{80}\right)}^{2} \\  & ≈130.7\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186385230 :question/problem "Consider the inexact differential equation

$$
xy\,\text{d}x-({x}^{2}+3{y}^{3})\,\text{d}y=0.
$$

It is known that 

$$
\frac{1}{P}(\frac{∂P}{∂y}-\frac{∂Q}{∂x})=\frac{3}{y}
$$

where the functions $P$ and $Q$ are given by 

$$
P(x,y)=xy,\,Q(x,y)=-{x}^{2}-3{y}^{3}.
$$

Use this information to find a suitable integrating factor $I(y)$ and hence find the general solution to the equation.

$\,$ A suitable integrating factor is $I(y)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The general solution is {{field-2}}, where $c$ is a constant."] [17592186385230 :question/worked-solution "For a differential equation of the form

$$
P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y=0,
$$

we have that if

$$
\frac{1}{P}(\frac{∂P}{∂y}-\frac{∂Q}{∂x})=h(y)
$$

where $h(y)$ is independent of $x,$ then an integrating factor for the equation is

$$
I(y)=\operatorname{exp}⁡(-\int h(y)\,\text{d}y)
$$

where $\operatorname{exp}⁡(y)$ denotes the exponential function ${e}^{y}.$

We are given that

$$
\frac{1}{P}(\frac{∂P}{∂y}-\frac{∂Q}{∂x})=\frac{3}{y}.
$$

Since $\frac{3}{y}$ is a function of $y$ only, we can conclude that the integrating factor for the equation is 

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x,y) & ={e}^{-\int 3/y\text{ }\text{d}y} \\  & ={e}^{-3\operatorname{ln}⁡y} \\  & =\frac{1}{{y}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying our equation by the integrating factor, we arrive at the following exact differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{{y}^{3}}(xy\,\text{d}x-({x}^{2}+3{y}^{3})\,\text{d}y) & =0 \\ \underbrace{\left(\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\right)}_{\overset{~}{P}}\,\text{d}x+\underbrace{(-1)(\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{3}}+3)}_{\overset{~}{Q}}\,\text{d}y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

For this exact equation, we have

$$
\overset{~}{P}(x,y)=\frac{x}{{y}^{2}},\,\overset{~}{Q}(x,y)=-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{3}}-3.
$$

To solve the equation, let's first integrate $\overset{~}{P}(x,y)$ with respect to $x.$
The result should include an arbitrary function of $y,$ which we'll call $F(y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(x,y) & =\int \overset{~}{P}(x,y)\,\text{d}x+F(y) \\  & =\int \frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+F(y) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2{y}^{2}}+F(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, let's integrate $\overset{~}{Q}(x,y)$ with respect to $y.$
The result should include an arbitrary function of $x,$ which we'll call $G(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(x,y) & =\int \overset{~}{Q}(x,y)\,\text{d}y+G(x) \\  & =\int (-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{3}}-3)\,\text{d}y+G(x) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2{y}^{2}}-3y+G(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Comparing the two solutions, we see that we must have

$$
F(y)=-3y,\,G(x)=0.
$$

Therefore, the general solution $u(x,y)=c$ is

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{2{y}^{2}}-3y=c.
$$"] [17592186385256 :question/worked-solution "Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$"] [17592186385927 :question/worked-solution "The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $8\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $20\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.1\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $10\,\text{H}.$

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

$$

$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$

$$"] [17592186385934 :question/worked-solution "The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $13\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $4\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.25\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $1\,\text{H}.$

First, we need to calculate $∇\times F.$ In doing so, we get

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}0.2 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & 0.4 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & 0.6\end{bmatrix}.

Notice that the matrix ${P}^{2}$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. 
As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}-0.8 & 0.2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0.4 & -0.6 & 0.4 & 0 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & -0.4 & 0\end{array}\right] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=5{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=5{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=\frac{5}{2}{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}-4 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 & 0\end{array}\right] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 2 & -3 & 2 & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+4{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & -4 & 0\end{array}\right] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain

$$

$$
\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\,400=1\,700.
$$"] [17592186388904 :question/worked-solution "Notice that the given curve is of the form $y=y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y=y(t)=2-\frac{t}{2}.$ This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$"] [17592186389490 :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina of mass $M$ and a line ${l}_{M}$ perpendicular to the lamina passing through its center of mass, the parallel axis theorem states that the moment of inertia of the lamina about a line $l$ parallel to ${l}_{M}$ is given by

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
